title: Season 2, Ep 4: The centralized prompt registry
oneliner: Split prompts into system prompts and app-generated prompts; version, test, and store both in a registry instead of burying them in code.
says: Organizations use prompts to call LLMs, and prompts fall into two categories: system prompts and application code-generated prompts. These must be decoupled. System prompts should be separated, tested, versioned, and deployed deliberately for good system performance. App-generated prompts also need separation, versioning, and storage in a repository, used properly whenever needed.
explained: Buried-in-code prompts are the spreadsheet chaos of the AI era (the same scattered mess uncontrolled spreadsheets cause): behavior-critical text scattered across repositories, edited by whoever, deployed whenever. The registry applies software discipline to it: prompts become managed artifacts with versions, tests, owners, and rollout control. When an update degrades answers, you can see what changed and roll back - impossible when the prompt was a string literal in three services.

The two-category split is the episode's sharp edge (its most important distinction). System prompts define how the model behaves - its persona, constraints, rules; they change rarely and deserve review like security policy. Application prompts are built at runtime from user input and context; they need templates and injection-safety checks. Treating them differently - governance heavy for the first, engineering rigor for the second - is what makes the registry practical instead of bureaucratic.
takeaway: Prompts are production artifacts: registry, versions, tests, owners. System prompts get policy-grade review; runtime prompts get engineering-grade templates.
